input:
Introduction

This report presents the design of an amine absorber and sets out the basis on which the design has been developed, the sizing of the column, the materials selected for construction, and the risks that remain open at this stage. The design throughput is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 93% of the key component in the feed gas. Wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel, and this selection is stated here in the basis so that the later sections can build on it.

Basis

The basis of the design is the starting point for everything that follows, and it is important that it is stated clearly and completely. The throughput and the duty are treated as fixed design values, and the sizing, materials and risks sections all work from these values. Only the design case is carried through the report: no second operating case is developed, and operation away from the design point is considered only where the risks section takes it up. The feed gas is treated as arriving at the absorber in the condition the design assumes, and the solvent is treated as the treating agent that removes the key component from the gas as the two streams pass through the column in contact with each other.

Sizing

The sizing of the absorber proceeds from the basis in a logical sequence. The diameter of the column is governed by the gas traffic at the design throughput, and the vapour velocity inside the column has to be kept comfortably below the point at which the liquid is carried back up the column and the separation breaks down. The height of the column is governed by the separation that the duty demands: the gas and the solvent have to remain in contact for long enough, and over enough transfer surface, for the removal to reach the specified level. The solvent circulation rate is closely linked to both of these, because it determines how much of the key component the solvent can take up as it passes through the column, and it also affects the liquid traffic that the internals have to handle. The pressure drop across the column is checked as part of the sizing, since it has an effect on the duty of the equipment around the absorber. Each of these elements interacts with the others, and the sizing represents a balanced position across all of them rather than the optimisation of any single one. It will be appreciated that the sizing is therefore an exercise in balance, and that changing any one element in isolation would tend to disturb the others.

Materials

The materials selection covers the wetted parts of the absorber, which are the parts that come into contact with the solvent and the process streams: the column shell, the internals, and the solvent pipework. Amine treating service is widely recognised as a demanding environment for materials, because the solvent, the products formed as the solvent degrades in service, and the wet gas itself can all attack materials that would perform perfectly well in other duties. The grade named in the basis has been selected to answer these challenges across the whole wetted envelope, so that no wetted surface is left as a weak point in the system. The welding and fabrication of the wetted parts are expected to preserve the corrosion resistance of the parent material, and the selection assumes that the completed equipment is inspected before it enters service. Parts of the equipment that never come into contact with the process fall outside the selection and are not covered by it.

Risks

Two risks are named in this report, and it should be emphasised that neither of them is resolved here. The first is fouling. Material can be deposited inside the column from several directions: solids entering with the feed gas, products formed as the solvent degrades, and products of corrosion within the system. As deposits build up, they can raise the pressure drop, disturb the distribution of the liquid, and reduce the quality of the contact between the gas and the solvent, so that the removal performance falls away from the design level. The second risk is turndown. The design is developed at a single design point, and the behaviour of the column at rates well below that point is not established: the solvent circulation and the distribution of liquid over the internals both change as the rate falls, and the removal duty cannot simply be assumed to hold. Both items remain open, and they are recorded here so that they are carried forward rather than lost. It is also fair to say that both risks are of a kind that tends to become apparent only in operation, which is precisely why they deserve to be recorded prominently at this stage rather than discovered later.
target:
Basis

This report covers the design of an amine absorber. The design throughput is 15 t per day. The duty is removal of 93% of the key component from the feed gas. Wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel; the selection is stated here, and the materials section works from it. The basis fixes the throughput and the duty as design values, and every later section works from these two figures. The design case is the only case sized in the report. Operation away from the design point is not sized; it is taken up as an open item in the risks section. The solvent removes the key component from the gas as the two streams pass through the column in contact. No sensitivity case stands in the basis: the report designs at the stated point, and a design at another throughput or another duty is a separate design.

Sizing

The column diameter is set by the gas traffic at the design throughput. The vapour velocity is held below the flooding limit with a margin, because at flooding the liquid is held up and carried back by the gas and the separation fails. The column height is set by the separation the duty requires: gas and solvent stay in contact over the height, and the removal reaches the specified level only if the contact surface and the contact time suffice. The solvent circulation rate is set by the loading the solvent reaches between its lean and rich ends, and it also fixes the liquid traffic the internals handle. The pressure drop across the column is calculated at the design point and checked against the driving force available from the equipment around the absorber. Diameter, height and circulation are coupled: a change in one moves the others, and the sizing states the position reached for all three together. Liquid distribution is part of the sizing. The solvent enters at the top and is spread over the internals, and the gas enters at the base and rises through it; maldistribution in either stream wastes contact surface, and the separation then falls short of the duty at the same geometry. The sizing proceeds in the standard sequence for an absorber: the traffic fixes the diameter, the separation fixes the height, and the solvent rate is set between them so that the loading stays within what the solvent reaches in this service.

Materials

The materials selection covers the wetted parts of the absorber: the column shell, the internals, and the solvent pipework. These are the surfaces in contact with the solvent and the process streams. Amine service attacks materials by three routes that act together: the solvent itself, the products formed as the solvent degrades in service, and the wet gas. A material that serves in a dry or a solvent-free duty is not evidence of performance here. The grade named in the basis is placed on every wetted surface, so the envelope has no surface of lower resistance. Welding of the wetted parts is specified to preserve the corrosion resistance of the parent material at the joints, and the selection assumes inspection of the completed wetted envelope before the equipment enters service. Parts that never contact the process stand outside the selection. The selection extends to the small wetted items as well as to the shell. Nozzles, distributors and supports see the same solvent and the same gas as the column wall, and a lesser material in a small part sets the corrosion life of the whole envelope.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling is the deposition of material inside the column, and the deposit has three sources in this service: solids entering with the feed gas, products of solvent degradation, and corrosion products from the system itself. A deposit raises the pressure drop, disturbs the distribution of liquid over the internals, and degrades the contact between gas and solvent; removal performance falls as the deposit grows. Turndown is the operation of the column at rates below the design point, and the design does not establish behaviour there. Solvent circulation falls with the gas rate, liquid distribution over the internals weakens, and the removal duty met at the design point is not met by default at the lower rate. The design is silent on both items beyond naming them, and each needs its own treatment before the design is relied on away from the design point or over a long campaign. No fouling allowance stands in the sizing, because no fouling rate for this service is established; a margin added without a rate behind it would be a guess in the form of a number. No turndown ratio is stated either. The lowest rate at which the column still meets the duty is a measured or a calculated quantity, and neither stands in the design as issued.
